awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Breath Monitoring Device to Detect Necrotizing Enterocolitis
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this I-Corps project is the development of a diagnostic device for the early detection of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) in premature newborn babies (neonates). By monitoring patient breath, this device has the potential to prevent deaths and comorbidities associated with NEC. Early detection of NEC could facilitate timely antibiotic treatment and could be lifesaving. Moreover, reducing clinicians' fear of NEC in patients presenting with common gastrointestinal symptoms could lead to better optimization of nutrition for all premature babies. If successful, this device could decrease neonatal mortality, lower the incidence of short bowel syndrome, improve neurodevelopmental outcomes, and shorten hospital stays by promoting faster growth.

This I-Corps project leverages experiential learning and direct investigation of the industry ecosystem to evaluate the translation potential of the technology. The solution builds upon the development of breath collection interfaces and gas sensor technologies to advance the clinical utility of breath biomarker research. Breath collection from premature neonates presents numerous challenges, including their high respiration rate, sample dilution due to respiratory support, and the fragility of their skin. By combining innovative breath collection techniques with highly responsive and sensitive gas sensors, these challenges can be effectively addressed, enabling real-time disease monitoring for clinicians.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a serious intestinal disease that mainly affects premature newborns. It causes part of the infant’s intestine to become inflamed and die, and it is a leading cause of illness and death among babies cared for in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). There is currently no reliable way to diagnose NEC early. Clinicians must often decide whether to start antibiotics or stop feeding a fragile infant without clear information. Our team is developing a non-invasive, continuous bedside monitor to help detect or rule out NEC sooner. This National Science Foundation Innovation Corps (I-Corps) award allowed us to test whether this technology meets a real clinical need and to understand what it would take to bring it to the infants who need it.
What we did: The team interviewed more than 100 stakeholders, including neonatologists, neonatal nurse practitioners, nurses, respiratory therapists, NICU medical directors, hospital administrators, members of hospital purchasing committees, and experienced medical device entrepreneurs. We visited rural, community, and academic NICUs in the United States, attended medical device development meetings, and traveled to hospitals in Spain and India to learn how newborn care and technology adoption differ around the world.
What we learned: Interviews confirmed strong interest in our technology among clinicians and hospital decision-makers, supporting continued development of both the device and a plan to bring it to market. Clinicians told us that their most important need is a reliable way to rule NEC out. They said a screening monitor would need to be correct more than 90% of the time when it reports that an infant does not have NEC. When a warning coincides with digestive symptoms, a lower level of certainty would still be valuable for flagging an infant for closer attention. This finding is now shaping how we set the device’s decision thresholds, how the monitor displays results to care teams, and which outcomes we will measure in future clinical studies. We also confirmed that a continuous monitor fits naturally into NICU routines, where clinicians already review bedside monitors, so it would add little to their workflow. Parents emerged as essential partners and advocates in this work.
We learned how hospitals decide to adopt new devices. Value analysis committees weigh patient benefit against cost. Hospital leaders focus on reducing costly complications and are also motivated by public NICU rankings, which reflect NEC outcomes. Insurers pay for hospital stays as bundles, so they are unlikely to reimburse the device separately, but they can help inform cost-effectiveness models. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s expectations will guide the device’s intended use and the clinical evidence needed. We also compared different ways of selling medical devices to hospitals and how each affects a company’s funding needs.
Internationally, clinicians in Spain shared the same concerns about NEC and used similar care practices. In India, health care is managed state by state, and new devices are often purchased through state tenders guided by local clinical leaders. District hospitals there run special newborn care units with many patients per nurse and few monitoring devices. These insights suggest that partnering with or licensing to local companies may be the best path to reach infants in such settings.
Intellectual Merit: This project produced new, evidence-based requirements for clinical adoption of non-invasive NEC monitoring, including the accuracy clinicians need, how results should be presented, and the cost and outcome evidence hospitals require. These findings will guide the design of clinical validation studies for our technology and for similar newborn technologies. They add to what is known about moving new neonatal technologies from the research lab into everyday care.
Broader Impacts: Earlier and more confident decisions about NEC could reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, needless feeding interruptions, surgeries, and long NICU stays. They could also lower the substantial health care costs of advanced NEC. By studying needs in rural, community, and international settings, we aim to ensure this technology can benefit infants in under-resourced hospitals, not only major academic centers. The project gave two early-career researchers intensive entrepreneurial training in customer discovery, market analysis, and communicating science to clinicians, administrators, and investors, along with a lasting network of mentors and collaborators. Our findings have been shared through pitch competitions supported by the FDA’s Pediatric Device Consortia, where the team won awards, and through our ongoing partnership with the NEC Society, an international patient advocacy organization. The NEC Society will serve as a patient and family advisory council, helping define the outcomes that matter most to families and sharing results with parents and clinicians.
